name: 1,8-cineole (eucalyptol)
short: Swallowed eucalyptus oil (mainly cineole) depressed consciousness in 28% of 109 hospitalised young children, some unconscious. In a COPD trial of cineole, adverse events were similar to placebo.
text: Cineole is the main constituent of eucalyptus oil, and the poisoning evidence below concerns eucalyptus oil rather than pure cineole. In a retrospective review of the case histories of 109 infants and young children admitted to a Melbourne hospital after swallowing eucalyptus oil, 59% had clinical effects: 28% had depressed consciousness (three were unconscious after 5 to 10 mL, and one was unconscious with hypoventilation after an estimated 75 mL), 37% vomited, 15% had ataxia and 11% had lung disease; all recovered, and the authors concluded that significant depression of consciousness should be anticipated after 5 mL or more of 100% oil and that minor depression of consciousness may occur after 2 to 3 mL. In contrast, in a retrospective case-note analysis of 41 children in south-east Queensland with oral eucalyptus oil poisoning, 80% had no symptoms, none needed advanced life support, and symptoms did not correlate with the amount taken. Two case reports of adults who unintentionally drank eucalyptus oil describe seizures and severe metabolic acidosis treated in intensive care; both were discharged on the fourth day. In trials of cineole capsules, adverse events were comparable with placebo over 6 months in 242 people with stable COPD randomised to 200 mg of cineole or placebo three times daily as add-on therapy, and in 152 people with acute rhinosinusitis mild side effects possibly related to treatment (heartburn and rash) occurred in two patients on cineole. In animal data, pregnant rats given 250 to 1000 mg/kg of cineole had a reduction in body weight, and the highest doses led to dead fetuses; the authors concluded that cineole possibly presents maternal and fetal toxicity. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
